1a.fix: Slide 8 of Chapter 1 (and page 12 of the book) calls the TRIP transformation endothermic and says it absorbs crash energy that way. The forward austenite-to-martensite transformation is exothermic: it gives out latent heat. The crash energy is absorbed as plastic work, because the strain-induced martensite raises the work-hardening rate and delays necking, so the sheet deforms much further before it fails.
1a.html:
Thick, soft low-carbon car bodies wasted fuel and raised pollution. A thinner panel saves weight only if the steel is stronger, yet it must still be deep drawn and stay crash safe, so the recipe had to give a high strength-to-weight ratio with formability.

  1. Carbon is the wrong route. Interstitial C distorts BCC ferrite and pins dislocations, and above a trace it forms pearlite: strength rises but drawability falls. Sheet steel must be almost pearlite-free.
  2. Interstitial-free (IF) steel. Vacuum degassing cuts C and N to a few tens of ppm; Ti or Nb fixes the rest. The clean ferrite deep draws excellently.
  3. P-added IF steel. About 0.1% P (0.12% in the course example) replaces Fe on lattice sites. This substitutional strengthening (about 62 MPa for 0.17% P) keeps drawability, so outer panels can be thinner.
  4. TRIP steel. Ferrite, bainite, martensite and retained austenite (RA). In a crash the RA turns to martensite, strength keeps rising and necking is delayed, so a thin part absorbs much energy. Used for rails, cross-members and pillars.

Strength now comes from substitutional solutes and multiphase structures, not carbon: lighter, safer cars.

1b.html:
Hydrogen enters steel as atoms: from moisture in the charge, slag and refractories during steelmaking, and from pickling, plating, welding consumables, cathodic protection or corrosion in service. It is far more soluble in liquid steel and austenite than in ferrite, so on cooling the excess diffuses to voids, inclusions, grain boundaries and highly stressed regions. There it recombines to \mathrm{H_2} (pressure) or lowers the cohesion of the lattice. The three panels show the three common results.

(1) Left: long crack along a plate or pipe: hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC).

  • Where: line pipe, pressure vessels and tanks of C-Mn plate in wet sour (\mathrm{H_2S}) service. \mathrm{H_2S} stops H atoms from the corrosion reaction pairing at the surface, so they enter the steel, collect at elongated MnS stringers and the hard, segregated centreline band, form \mathrm{H_2} and crack the plate parallel to its surface in linked steps; near the surface they raise blisters.
  • Remedy: S below about 0.002% with Ca treatment (globular sulphides), low centreline segregation, controlled rolling and accelerated cooling (no hard bands), hardness at most 22 HRC, HIC-tested plate; coatings and inhibitors.

(2) Middle: cracked, flaking billet: hydrogen flakes and breakout.

  • Where: continuously cast billets and blooms, heavy forgings and rails. H dissolved in the liquid is rejected on solidification and again on \gamma \to \alpha; it forms \mathrm{H_2} in pores, and the gas pressure plus thermal stress cracks the section, flakes out the billet surface, or breaks out the shell in the caster.
  • Remedy: dry scrap, ferroalloys, fluxes and ladle linings; vacuum degassing to below about 2 ppm H; slow (pit or stack) cooling or an anti-flake hold at about 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} so H diffuses out before the steel is cold.

(3) Right: intergranular fracture: hydrogen embrittlement (delayed fracture).

  • Where: high-strength steel above about 1000 MPa: bolts and springs after acid pickling or electroplating, hardened gears, and the weld heat-affected zone (cold cracking from damp electrodes). A few ppm H collect at stressed prior-austenite grain boundaries; the part cracks hours or days after loading below its yield stress. Elongation and reduction of area fall, YS and UTS do not.
  • Remedy: bake about 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for several hours within a few hours of plating; inhibited pickling or blast cleaning; keep hardness down; for welds use dried low-hydrogen electrodes, preheat and post-heat (about 200 to 250^\circ\mathrm{C}).

At high temperature, H attacks carbides to form methane; Cr-Mo steels resist this and are used where H is known to be present.

2a.html:
Silicon deoxidises steel and strengthens ferrite, but it raises the DBTT, adds to temper embrittlement and harms coatings and welds.

  1. Hot-dip galvanised steel (structural sections, sheet, wire). Above about 0.04% Si the Fe-Zn reaction speeds up: even 0.04 against 0.06% Si gives a much thicker, dull, brittle, poorly adherent coating. Si is kept below about 0.04%.
  2. Welded steels. Si spoils the weld surface and aggravates cracking when C is fairly high, so Si is held at 0.10% or less for best weldability.

Phosphorus is the most potent solid-solution strengthener of ferrite (0.17% P adds about 62 MPa to YS and UTS) and aids machinability and atmospheric corrosion resistance, but it segregates to grain boundaries.

  1. Quenched and tempered low-alloy and HSLA steels (shafts, rotors, pressure parts). P segregates to prior-austenite grain boundaries during tempering or slow cooling through about 375 to 575^\circ\mathrm{C}: temper embrittlement, with fracture changing from transgranular cleavage to intergranular. Limit 0.02%, and below 0.01% for low and moderately high (about 400^\circ\mathrm{C}) temperature service.
  2. Galvanised and deep-drawn sheet. Above 0.04% P the Fe-Zn layer grows fast and the coating is rough, brittle and poorly adherent. In deep-drawing steel that is later reheated, P below 0.01% avoids secondary work embrittlement.

2b.html:
Why S forms compounds. Extensive solid solution needs the Hume-Rothery conditions, and S fails them:

  • Size: the S atom (about 0.104 nm) is about 16% smaller than Fe (0.124 nm). That is beyond the 15% limit for substitution, yet far too large for the interstitial holes of iron (at most about 0.053 nm in FCC and 0.036 nm in BCC).
  • Electronegativity: S (2.58) is much more electronegative than Fe (1.83) and Mn (1.55). A large difference favours a compound over a solid solution.
  • Valence and structure: S is a non-metal that takes two electrons (\mathrm{S^{2-}}) and does not share the metallic BCC or FCC structure of iron.

So S is almost insoluble in solid iron (hundredths of a percent at most, practically nil at room temperature). The 0.01 to 0.05% S of steel is pushed into the last liquid and freezes as sulphides. MnS is more stable than FeS, so S goes to Mn first and forms FeS only when Mn is short.

The two inclusions in the figure

  • FeS: the continuous dark films outlining the grains. It forms when Mn is too low and wets the grain boundaries.
  • MnS (or (Mn,Fe)S): the isolated globular and irregular particles inside the grains. It forms as discrete particles, melts at about 1610^\circ\mathrm{C} and is randomly distributed, not on the boundaries.

Effects in metal working

FeS: hot shortness. FeS melts at 1194^\circ\mathrm{C} and its eutectic with iron at about 988^\circ\mathrm{C}, below the hot-rolling and forging range (about 1000 to 1250^\circ\mathrm{C}). The boundary film is liquid or very weak, so the grains separate: red (hot) shortness, edge cracks and tearing in rolling and forging. Cure: Mn/S of at least 8, which converts S to MnS, and desulphurisation.

MnS: anisotropy. MnS causes no hot shortness, but it is plastic at working temperatures and elongates into stringers along the rolling direction in both hot and cold rolling. The stringers carry no load, so across the rolling direction the tensile strength, ductility, impact energy and fatigue life fall (transverse fatigue strength about half the longitudinal at 10^8 cycles). Thick plates suffer lamellar tearing under welds, and sheet splits when bent across the stringers.

MnS in machining is useful: it breaks chips and gives a better finish, so free-cutting (resulphurised) steels carry 0.08 to 0.33% S.

Control: low S plus Ca or rare-earth treatment, which makes hard, globular sulphides that do not elongate.

The figure is the steel corner of the metastable Fe-\mathrm{Fe_3C} diagram (0 to about 2.1% C).

Labels. Temperature (^\circ\mathrm{C}) against wt% C. Left-axis point: 912^\circ\mathrm{C} (\alpha \to \gamma of pure iron). Line from it to the V: A_3. Short line from it to P (0.022% C, maximum C in ferrite) and the curve below P: \alpha/(\alpha+\gamma) boundary and solvus of C in ferrite (0.008% C at room temperature). Horizontal: A_1, eutectoid isotherm, 727^\circ\mathrm{C}. V point: eutectoid S, 0.76% C. Rising line: A_{cm}, to 2.14% C at 1147^\circ\mathrm{C}. Fields: \gamma; \alpha+\gamma; \alpha; \gamma+\mathrm{Fe_3C}; below A_1, proeutectoid ferrite + pearlite (hypoeutectoid) and proeutectoid cementite + pearlite (hypereutectoid).

Annealing by composition

  1. Full annealing, hypoeutectoid steels: 30 to 40^\circ\mathrm{C} above A_3, furnace cool at 20 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C/h}: coarse pearlite + ferrite, softest, for machining castings and forgings. Hypereutectoid steels go only 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C} above A_1, never above A_{cm}: slow cooling from there leaves a brittle cementite network.
  2. Spheroidising, high-C and hypereutectoid tool and bearing steels: 15 to 25 h just below A_1, or cycling about A_1: globular \mathrm{Fe_3C}, maximum machinability and formability, good start for hardening.
  3. Process annealing, low-C cold-worked sheet and wire: below A_1; recrystallisation restores ductility between passes.
  4. Stress relief, any composition: below A_1, no phase change; for welded, cast and machined parts.

3b.html:
Given: plain carbon steel, 0.20% C (Mn taken as 0.45%, Si 0.25%, as in AISI 1020); shaft diameter 500 mm; as-quenched hardness 45 HRC at the surface, 40 HRC in the next ring, 30 HRC at the core.

Find: the martensite each zone needs, the hardening temperatures and times, and the schedule drawn on a TTT diagram.

Step 1. Martensite needed (hardness against dissolved carbon, slide 22):

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} &= 35 + 50(0.20) = 45 \\ \mathrm{HRC_{90}} &= 30 + 50(0.20) = 40 \\ \mathrm{HRC_{50}} &= 23 + 50(0.20) = 33 \end{aligned}

The surface must be fully (99.9%) martensitic, the ring 90% martensite, and the core about 50% martensite (33 HRC covers 30 HRC) with bainite and fine pearlite. 45 HRC is the ceiling for 0.20% C, so the surface has no margin.

Step 2. Austenitising temperature:

\begin{aligned} A_3 &= 910 - 203\sqrt{0.20} \approx 819^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ T_{\gamma} &= A_3 + (30\ \text{to}\ 50) \approx 870^\circ\mathrm{C} \end{aligned}

Full austenite is essential: any free ferrite caps the surface below 45 HRC.

Step 3. Heating and soaking. \mathrm{CE} = \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{Mn}/5 + (\mathrm{Si} - 0.5)/5 \approx 0.24 < 0.4, so the steel is not crack sensitive, but a 500 mm section must pass 250 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} slowly: preheat at about 650^\circ\mathrm{C} until the core equalises, then heat to 870^\circ\mathrm{C} in a protective atmosphere (decarburisation would lose the 45 HRC skin). Soak

t = 60 + D = 60 + 500 = 560\ \mathrm{min} \approx 9.5\ \mathrm{h}

Step 4. Quench. M_s = 520 - 320(0.20) - 50(0.45) \approx 433^\circ\mathrm{C}; M_f \approx 265^\circ\mathrm{C} (read from book Fig 2.53). The ferrite and pearlite nose of a 0.2% C steel lies near 550 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} at under 1 s, so use the most severe quench: 10% brine, violent agitation (H = 5), or a water spray, with the shaft lowered vertically. On the TTT diagram:

  • surface curve misses the nose: 99.9% M, 45 HRC;
  • ring curve grazes the start curve: about 10% ferrite + bainite, 90% M, 40 HRC;
  • core curve crosses the 50% line: about 50% M + bainite and fine pearlite, 30 to 33 HRC.

Step 5. Temper at once at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C} (about 1 h per 25 mm): quench stresses fall while lath martensite of 0.2% C loses only 1 to 2 HRC.

Step 6. Feasibility (Grossmann). For 0.20% C, ASTM 7: D_I \approx 0.16 \times 2.5\,(\mathrm{Mn}) \approx 0.4 in, so in brine the critical diameter is only about 0.3 in (7 mm). A 50% martensite core at 500 mm (19.7 in) needs D_I \approx 20 in, fifty times more. As slide 43 warns, steels below about 0.25% C cannot be through-hardened by a practical quench: in this shaft the 45 and 40 HRC zones form only as a skin a few mm thick and the core stays ferrite + pearlite (below 20 HRC).

Answer: austenitise at about 870^\circ\mathrm{C} (9.5 h soak after preheat), quench in agitated brine, temper at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C}. To meet the drawn depths, keep 0.20% C (it fixes the hardness values) but use a deep-hardening Ni-Cr-Mo steel, or make the hard zones by surface hardening.

4b.html:
Cold treatment against cryotreatment

Both are sub-zero steps given right after quenching and before tempering, but they act on different things.

Cold treatmentCryotreatment
Cycle-70 to -120^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 1 h per 3 cm of section-135^\circ\mathrm{C} and below (liquid \mathrm{N_2}, -196^\circ\mathrm{C}), 24 h or longer
Changeretained austenite (RA) to martensiteRA to martensite, plus conditioning of the martensite
Wear gain frommainly hardnesshardness and many more fine carbides
  • Cold treatment takes the steel below M_f, so the soft, unstable RA becomes martensite. Hardness and dimensional stability rise, and wear resistance rises with hardness. Some RA is left on purpose in bearings and gears for toughness.
  • Cryotreatment also removes RA, but the long deep soak contracts the lattice and creates defect sites in the martensite. On tempering these nucleate fine, coherent transition carbides. The carbide count rises steadily as the soak gets colder and longer (D2, slide 54: about 32,300 per \mathrm{mm^2} at +20^\circ\mathrm{C}, 35,000 at -80^\circ\mathrm{C}, 37,900 at -180^\circ\mathrm{C}), so cold treatment gets only part of this gain. Fine carbides resist abrasion without lowering toughness: tool life rises 2 to 5 times and one temper is enough.

The stress figure

Arrows show expansion (outward) or contraction (inward) of the surface (solid) and centre (dashed) of a quenched bar.

  • (a) Uniform heating: surface and centre both expand; no stress.
  • (b) Start of quench: the surface cools and contracts first, so surface in tension, centre in compression. Elastically S = \alpha E\Delta T: with \alpha \approx 12\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} and E \approx 200 GPa, each 100^\circ\mathrm{C} of surface-centre difference means about 240 MPa.
  • (c) Midway: the surface passes M_s and becomes martensite, about 4% larger in volume than austenite, so it expands while the hot centre still contracts: surface in compression, centre in tension.
  • (d) Near the end: the surface is cold, rigid martensite; the centre now transforms and expands, putting the brittle surface into tension: distortion and quench cracks.

Why it matters more in hardening. A quench gives surface-centre differences of hundreds of degrees, and the expansion happens at different times at low temperature, where the steel cannot relax by flow. In normalising, still air keeps the difference to tens of degrees and austenite turns to ferrite and pearlite at about 550 to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, where stresses relax plastically. Normalising even removes stresses.

Hardening schedule: normalise or stress relieve first; heat slowly through 250 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} with a preheat for complex or crack-sensitive parts; austenitise only \mathrm{A_3} (hypo) or \mathrm{A_1} (hyper) + 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C}; quench in the mildest medium that beats the critical rate (oil or polymer for intricate shapes); dip along the long axis with uniform agitation; martemper just above M_s to remove (c) and (d); temper at once.

Normalising schedule: \mathrm{A_3} or \mathrm{A_{cm}} + 50 to 60^\circ\mathrm{C}, soak (about 60 + D min, D in mm), cool in still air with the part well supported.

5a.html:
Principle. The austenite of solution-annealed 304L is metastable: M_s is below room temperature but M_d is above it, so plastic strain turns part of it into \alpha' martensite (BCC, ferromagnetic, 2.57% volume increase). The hard \alpha' raises the work-hardening rate and strength (TRIP effect).

Given: V_{\gamma,0} = 0.95 before the step (the balance taken as \delta-ferrite); required V_{\alpha'} = 0.10.

Assumed: Ludwigson-Berger relation (slide 23) with A_1 \approx 1 and B \approx 3 for stainless steels; \varepsilon is the true strain; deformation at room temperature; V_\gamma is the austenite left after the step.

Find: strain \varepsilon.

Step 1. Feasibility. Typical 304L (0.02 C + 0.05 N, 18.5 Cr, 9 Ni, 1.5 Mn, 0.5 Si):

M_{d30} = 413 - 13.7(18.5) - 9.5(9) - 8.1(1.5) - 9.2(0.5) - 462(0.07) \approx 25^\circ\mathrm{C}

Room temperature is at or below M_d, so straining forms \alpha'.

Step 2. Remaining austenite:

V_\gamma = 0.95 - 0.10 = 0.85

Step 3. Solve for strain:

\begin{aligned} V_{\alpha'} &= A_1\,\varepsilon^{B}\,V_\gamma \\ \varepsilon &= \left(\frac{V_{\alpha'}}{A_1 V_\gamma}\right)^{1/B} = \left(\frac{0.10}{1 \times 0.85}\right)^{1/3} = (0.1176)^{1/3} \end{aligned}

Answer: true strain \varepsilon \approx 0.49 (about 63% engineering strain in tension). Taking V_\gamma = 0.95 instead gives 0.47.

Comment. This is close to the forming limit of 304L, so the step is best done slightly below room temperature, where the austenite is less stable and less strain gives the same martensite. Forming makes the part slightly magnetic.

5b.html:
Cause: 475 C embrittlement of the ferrite

Reading Figure 5(b). The ferrite (F) regions are flat cleavage facets with river-like lines; only the austenite (A) islands show bright, torn ridges of ductile (dimple) fracture. The ferrite has become brittle and the austenite alone carries the ductility.

Cause. This is the fractograph of 475 C embrittlement: precipitation of Cr-rich \alpha' in the ferrite during exposure in the range 350 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} (maximum near 475^\circ\mathrm{C}). Fe-Cr ferrite decomposes into Fe-rich \alpha and Cr-rich \alpha', which is cubic, nanometre-sized, coherent with the ferrite and very resistant to coarsening. Its coherency strain blocks dislocations, so the ferrite hardens and fails by cleavage. Higher Cr, and hence more ferrite, makes the steel more sensitive. In the pilot run the parts were most likely cooled slowly (air or furnace) after solution annealing, or stress relieved or welded, through this range.

Sigma, chi, \mathrm{Cr_2N} or \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} (600 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C}) would instead appear as particles at the \alpha/\gamma boundaries, with cracks running along them.

Confirm: ferrite microhardness and Charpy energy; etch for sigma (none expected); \alpha' is too fine for SEM and needs TEM; check the ferrite fraction (about 50%, never below 30%).

Remedy using the TTT diagram (slide 26)

From the figure: the \mathrm{Cr_2N}/chi/\mathrm{M_{23}C_6} nose is at about 850^\circ\mathrm{C} after about 2 min, the sigma nose about 800^\circ\mathrm{C} after about 20 min, and the \alpha' (475 C) nose about 480^\circ\mathrm{C} after about 20 min.

  1. Re-solution anneal at about 1050^\circ\mathrm{C} (1020 to 1100^\circ\mathrm{C}): \alpha' and any sigma dissolve, and the 50/50 \alpha/\gamma balance is restored.
  2. Water quench, so the cooling path passes left of every nose: through 1000 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} in well under 2 min, and through 550 to 350^\circ\mathrm{C} in seconds. Air cooling of thick sections cuts the noses.
  3. Prevent recurrence: no stress relief or hot forming between about 300 and 1000^\circ\mathrm{C}; service below about 250^\circ\mathrm{C}; solution anneal and quench after welding; keep Cr, Ni and N balanced so ferrite stays near 50%.

6a.html:
Choice: pack boronizing (boriding). It is the only diffusion treatment in the course that meets all three demands on a mild steel:

RequirementBoride layer (Fe2B, FeB)
Extremely high hardnessabout 1500 to 2000 HV, far above carburised martensite (700 to 800 HV)
Acidic corrosioninert boride; resists non-oxidising acids (HCl, H2SO4, H3PO4)
Hot hardness and wearhardness kept up to about 650^\circ\mathrm{C}; low friction

Carburised martensite softens above about 200^\circ\mathrm{C}. Nitriding needs Al, Cr or V: on plain mild steel it gives only a thin iron-nitride white layer over a soft diffusion zone. Chromizing forms hard Cr carbide only with at least 0.35% C. Low-carbon steel gives the thickest saw-tooth boride layer, keyed into the core.

Outline (pack boronizing):

  1. Degrease the blades; use a preconditioned (pre-borided) steel box.
  2. Pack: SiC layer, boronizing mix (B4C source, KBF4 activator, SiC diluent), blades, mix, SiC, then 20 to 25 mm of glass powder to seal out air.
  3. Hold at 900 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C} (typically 950^\circ\mathrm{C}) for 2 to 6 h. Fe2B nucleates at surface defects and grows as columns, X^2 = kt; FeB forms on top if the boron potential is high.
  4. Air cool, then diffusion anneal to convert FeB to single-phase Fe2B (about 50 to 200 \mum).

Limitations:

  • Cost: high (slide 35): a long high-temperature cycle, consumable B4C packs, labour-intensive packing and unpacking; finishing only by diamond grinding or lapping.
  • Processing: layer thickness is hard to control; the layer grows outward, so dimensions change; thin blades distort and mild-steel austenite grains coarsen during hours at 950^\circ\mathrm{C} (above Ac3), so a normalise may be needed; masking for selective areas; liquid and gas routes are toxic, so pack is used.
  • Metallurgical compatibility: FeB is brittle and in residual tension, Fe2B in compression, so a dual layer cracks and spalls under thermal cycling. The soft core (about 150 HV) cannot support a 2000 HV skin under contact load (eggshell effect). Si and Al are rejected ahead of the layer; above 0.8% in total they leave a soft ferrite band beneath. Boron at grain boundaries embrittles.

Conclusion: boronize, aiming for a single-phase Fe2B layer; the high cost is repaid by long life.

6b.html:
Diagnosis. Figure 6(b) is direct hardening (type A, slide 20): the gear is quenched straight from the carburising temperature (the dashed line only pre-cools it slightly). After the long hold at about 920 to 950^\circ\mathrm{C} the austenite of case and core is coarse, and it is quenched from the highest temperature. The result is coarse high-carbon plate martensite with much retained austenite, and the largest thermal and transformation stresses in a big section: cracking and warping.

Proposed schedule: cycle B of slide 20 (isothermal transformation, then a single reheat and quench)

  1. Carburise as before, about 925^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Cool in the furnace or a pit to about 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}, below A_1, and hold until the coarse austenite has transformed to ferrite + pearlite. Do not cool to room temperature.
  3. Reheat to just above \mathrm{Ac_3} of the case, about 800 to 820^\circ\mathrm{C} (below \mathrm{Ac_3} of the core), and equalise.
  4. Quench in agitated oil, or hot oil at 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for this large gear.
  5. Temper at once at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C}.

How it solves the problems

  • Fine grains: the \gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \mathrm{P} \rightarrow \gamma cycle renucleates austenite at many sites, so the case martensite is fine: tougher and less crack-prone.
  • Lower quench temperature: about 810^\circ\mathrm{C} instead of 925^\circ\mathrm{C} cuts the thermal gradient and stress, so less warping; less dissolved carbon means less retained austenite.
  • Milder quench: the high-carbon case has ample hardenability, so oil or hot oil is enough.
  • Tough core: heated between A_1 and A_3, it becomes fine ferrite with low-carbon martensite or bainite.
  • Economy: the part stays hot and is reheated by only about 200^\circ\mathrm{C} in the same line; types C and D (cooling to room temperature, one or two full reheats) cost more and are kept for parts that still crack.

Grain refinement mechanism: austenite to ferrite + pearlite to new austenite gives fine grains and fine martensite
Lower quenching temperature and milder quench reduce gradient, stress and retained austenite, so less warping and cracking

Economy: no cooling to room temperature, one short reheat; types C and D cost more

7a.html:
No. Vanadium will raise the hot hardness and wear resistance of the tungsten-based Unit A far more than that of the molybdenum-based Unit B, and in both only if carbon is raised with it.

Why the tools wear. In high-speed machining the cutting edge reaches about 500 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}. Wear is abrasion plus softening of the edge. It is resisted by hard undissolved carbides and by secondary hardening: on tempering at about 550^\circ\mathrm{C} fine alloy carbides precipitate in the martensite and retained austenite turns to martensite on cooling, so the steel keeps its red hardness.

What V does.

  • It forms MC (VC), the hardest carbide: about 3000 HV against 2000 for \mathrm{M_2C} and 1500 for \mathrm{M_6C}.
  • Dissolved V re-precipitates as an ultrafine VC dispersion: the strongest, most coarsening-resistant secondary peak. About 2% V gives a peak as high as 5% Mo, while 20% W gives only a plateau (Fig. 4.25 of the course book).
  • VC dissolves only at very high austenitising temperatures; undissolved VC resists abrasion but adds nothing to secondary hardening.
  • V is a carbon sink: 1% V ties up about 0.21% C, against 0.063% for Mo and 0.033% for W (equivalent alloy = \%\mathrm{W} + 1.9\,\%\mathrm{Mo} + 6.3\,\%\mathrm{V}, divided by 30 for carbon).

Unit A (T type, for example T1: 18W-4Cr-1V-0.75C). \mathrm{W_2C} gives only a weak, broad secondary hardening. T steels are hardened from 1260 to 1300^\circ\mathrm{C}, so most added V dissolves and precipitates as VC at 550 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}: the peak rises and moves to higher temperature, and the extra MC adds abrasion resistance. Strongly effective (the T15 route).

Unit B (M type, for example M2: 6W-5Mo-2V-4Cr-0.85C). \mathrm{Mo_2C} already gives a sharp peak near 550^\circ\mathrm{C}. M steels are hardened lower, 1190 to 1230^\circ\mathrm{C}, so much extra V stays as primary MC: wear improves, secondary hardening little. Without extra carbon VC robs the \mathrm{Mo_2C} and the martensite, so hardness can even fall; M steels also decarburise easily, starving the edge.

Recommendation. Unit A: 1 to 2% more V with about 0.2% C per 1% V, triple tempered at 550 to 560^\circ\mathrm{C}. Unit B: V only with balanced carbon (M3 or M4 type, 3 to 4% V, 1.05 to 1.3% C), hardened in salt bath or vacuum; for red hardness add Co (M42).

7b.html:
Given: M7 high-speed steel with 8.75% Mo, 1.72% W and 2% V (wt%).

Find: the minimum carbon content.

Principle (carbon balance). Each carbide former must find enough carbon to form its carbide (MC, \mathrm{M_2C}, \mathrm{M_6C}), which gives wear resistance and secondary hardening, and some carbon must stay in solution to give hard martensite. The course weights each element by the carbon it binds, as an equivalent alloy content.

Step 1. Equivalent alloy content

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{EA} &= \%\mathrm{W} + 1.9\,\%\mathrm{Mo} + 6.3\,\%\mathrm{V} \\ &= 1.72 + 1.9(8.75) + 6.3(2.0) = 1.72 + 16.63 + 12.60 = 30.95\ \mathrm{wt\%} \end{aligned}

Step 2. Equivalent carbon (carbon tied up as carbides)

C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{\mathrm{EA}}{30} = \frac{30.95}{30} = 1.03\ \mathrm{wt\%}

Step 3. Service requirement. Steels alloyed with W, Mo and V should contain 0.1 to 0.2% C more than C_{\mathrm{eq}}, so the matrix keeps carbon for martensite:

C = 1.03 + (0.1\ \text{to}\ 0.2) = 1.13\ \text{to}\ 1.23\ \mathrm{wt\%}

Stoichiometric check. The weights are the carbon bound per 1% of each element: W in \mathrm{W_2C}, 12.01/(2 \times 183.84) = 0.033 (= 1/30); Mo in \mathrm{Mo_2C}, 12.01/(2 \times 95.95) = 0.063 (= 1.9/30); V in VC, 12.01/50.94 = 0.236 (the rule uses 6.3/30 = 0.21). Then 1.72(0.033) + 8.75(0.063) + 2(0.236) = 1.07\%, close to C_{\mathrm{eq}}.

Answer: C_{\mathrm{eq}} = 1.03 wt%, so the minimum carbon for good service is about 1.13 wt% (1.13 to 1.23 wt%). With less, V and Mo carbides rob the matrix of carbon: soft martensite and weak secondary hardening. With much more, retained austenite and coarse carbides cost toughness.
pts: States the carbon balance: carbon must form carbides with W, Mo and V and still leave carbon in the martensite
Equivalent alloy content \%\mathrm{W} + 1.9\,\%\mathrm{Mo} + 6.3\,\%\mathrm{V} = 30.95 wt%
Equivalent carbon = \mathrm{EA}/30 = 1.03 wt%
Adds the 0.1 to 0.2% excess required for service properties: 1.13 to 1.23 wt%
Final answer with unit: minimum about 1.13 wt% C (C_{\mathrm{eq}} 1.03 wt%)
Explains the weights (carbon per % of element in \mathrm{M_2C} and MC, about 1.07% by stoichiometry) or the effect of too little and too much carbon

• "Minimum required carbon" can be read as C_{\mathrm{eq}} itself (1.03 wt%) or as C_{\mathrm{eq}} + 0.1 (1.13 wt%); state both, as above, and say which rule gives each.
  • Cr (about 4% in all M grades) is not in the formula: its carbides dissolve during austenitising and it serves mainly hardenability.
  • Slide 10 lists M7 at 1.00% C, just under C_{\mathrm{eq}}; the course rule is a recommendation for the best hardness and red hardness (high-carbon variants of the M grades exist), not a statement that M7 is mis-specified.
  • Do not divide by 30 before weighting: the factors 1.9 and 6.3 express that 1% Mo or V binds 1.9 or 6.3 times as much carbon as 1% W.

Recommendation: ferritic ductile (nodular, SG) iron of the low-temperature type, grade 60-40-18 (about 414 MPa UTS, 276 MPa YS, 18% elongation), made by a full anneal of a low-Si iron.

Why:

  1. Graphite shape. Spheroids are not notches; they blunt and arrest cracks (slide 3), so the matrix decides the toughness. Grey iron's flakes act as sharp internal cracks (practically no elongation), and white iron is massive cementite: both fail by brittle fracture.
  2. Matrix. A carbide-free ferrite matrix has the lowest ductile-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) and the highest impact energy of the usual matrices (ferrite, pearlite, tempered martensite). Pearlite, carbides and martensite raise the DBTT.
  3. Composition. Si raises the DBTT and lowers impact energy (slide 4), so Si is kept at the low end (about 2%). P is kept very low because it causes cold shortness (slide 5). Low Mn and no Cr avoid pearlite and carbides. Up to about 1% Ni restores strength without lowering impact (slide 5).
  4. Section. Hydraulic blocks are thick, pressure-tight castings. Ductile iron can be cast in any section. Malleable iron also has good low-temperature toughness (book p 312), but it must first solidify white, so it is limited to thin sections.

Heat-treatment cycle (full anneal for low-Si iron, slide 10):

  1. Heat slowly to 870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} and hold only to equalise (about 1 h per inch of section). If the casting has carbides, use the graphitising anneal instead: 900 to 925^\circ\mathrm{C} for at least 2 h.
  2. Furnace cool at 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}. Through the critical range (about 790 to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}), carbon diffuses out of the austenite onto the nodules, so the austenite becomes ferrite rather than pearlite.
  3. Air cool from 345^\circ\mathrm{C}.

The result is a fully ferritic, carbide-free matrix with nodules: grade 60-40-18 with the maximum low-temperature impact strength. Slow cooling through 350 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} embrittles irons high in Si and P (slide 16), so both are kept low. Qualify the casting by Charpy tests at the service temperature (for example -40^\circ\mathrm{C}).
pts: Recommends ferritic ductile iron (low-temperature type, grade 60-40-18), produced by annealing (blackheart ferritic malleable iron, argued from its low Si and low DBTT, also earns this point)
Spheroidal graphite: no notch effect, crack arrester; rejects grey iron (flakes, no elongation) and white iron (cementite)
A fully ferritic, carbide-free matrix gives the lowest DBTT and the highest impact energy; pearlite, carbides and martensite raise the DBTT
Composition: low Si (Si raises the DBTT), very low P (cold shortness), low Mn and no Cr; Ni for strength
Thick pressure block: ductile iron casts in any section; malleable iron is limited to thin sections

Cycle step 1: austenitise at 870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} and equalise (graphitising anneal at 900 to 925^\circ\mathrm{C} for at least 2 h if carbides are present); for malleable iron, slow heating of white iron to about 900^\circ\mathrm{C} and a long hold to form temper carbon

Cycle steps 2 and 3: furnace cool at 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}, then air cool; carbon deposits on the nodules, leaving ferrite (for malleable iron: very slow cooling through the critical range to a ferritic, blackheart matrix)
Guards against temper embrittlement (low Si and P) and qualifies by low-temperature Charpy tests

8a.watch:
• Malleable iron is a defensible second answer: course book p 312 says it has better low-temperature fracture toughness and a lower DBTT than nodular irons because of its lower Si, and it is made by the slide 19 cycle (slow heating of white iron to about 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, long hold, very slow cooling for blackheart ferrite). It suits a thick block poorly because it must first solidify white, so give the section reason whichever you choose.
  • Austenitic (high-Ni) ductile iron stays tough down to cryogenic temperatures, but it is costly and weaker in yield. It is the choice only for far colder service.
  • Slide 10's cooling (furnace cool to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}) passes slowly through the 350 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} embrittlement range of slide 16. This is safe only when P and Si are low. Otherwise air cool once the matrix is fully ferritic, at about 650^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  • The grade figures (60-40-18 is 60 ksi UTS, 40 ksi YS, 18% elongation) are the ASTM A536 designation that the slide uses.

8b.fix: Slide 18 (and book p 309) print the dislocation term as 7.34\times10^{-6}\rho and give the lath width d in mm. The term is 7.34\times10^{-6}\rho^{1/2}, which is Taylor hardening 0.38\,\mu b\sqrt{\rho} with \rho in \mathrm{m^{-2}}: the slide's own \log\rho relation gives \rho \approx 5.5\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}} at 623 K, so about 545 MPa, whereas 7.34\times10^{-6}\rho would give 4\times10^{10} MPa. Likewise 115\,d^{-1} needs d in \mu\mathrm{m}: laths 0.2 to 1 \mu\mathrm{m} wide give 575 to 115 MPa, while d in mm would give 10^{5} MPa or more.
8b.html:
Microstructure: ausferrite. ADI has graphite nodules in a matrix of fine, acicular bainitic ferrite and high-carbon retained austenite (about 1.8 to 2.2% C, 20 to 40% of the matrix), with no carbide. Its toughness comes from four features (slide 17; book p 308):

  1. No carbides. The 2 to 3% Si of ductile iron suppresses cementite precipitation. The carbon rejected by the growing ferrite therefore enriches the surrounding austenite instead of forming the brittle carbide films of steel bainite.
  2. Finer ferrite. The ferrite laths are very fine. Fine laths raise strength (the 115\,d^{-1} term of slide 18) and deflect cracks, so strength and toughness rise together.
  3. Stable high-carbon austenite. With about 2% C its M_s lies far below room temperature, so the FCC austenite stays tough even at low temperature. It strain hardens strongly and, under high local strain, can transform to martensite, which blunts crack tips and spreads the deformation.
  4. Graphite spheroids still act as crack arresters.

The result is about twice the strength of conventional ductile iron at the same elongation (slide 17): about 900 MPa UTS at 9% elongation, against 450 to 500 MPa for ordinary ductile iron. ADI matches forged steel at about 10% lower density and lower cost.

Heat-treatment schedule (slide 17; book Fig 6.13):

  1. Austenitise at 850 to 950^\circ\mathrm{C} (slide range 800 to 950^\circ\mathrm{C}) in a chloride salt bath (KCl, NaCl, \mathrm{BaCl_2}) for about 1 to 2 h, until the matrix is fully austenitic. Temperature and Si fix its carbon: \%C_0 = T/420 - 0.17\,\mathrm{Si} - 0.95.
  2. Quench fast into a nitrate salt bath (\mathrm{KNO_3} and \mathrm{NaNO_3}) at 250 to 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, missing the pearlite nose. Heavy sections need Mo, Ni or Cu for austemperability.
  3. Hold isothermally, typically 1 to 2 h. Stage I is \gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \gamma_{\mathrm{HC}} (high-carbon austenite). End the hold inside the processing window. Too short a hold leaves low-carbon austenite that forms martensite on cooling. Too long a hold starts stage II, \gamma_{\mathrm{HC}} \rightarrow \alpha + \text{carbide}, which embrittles.
  4. Air cool. No tempering is needed.

Bath temperature sets the grade. At 250 to 300^\circ\mathrm{C}, fine ferrite and little austenite give the highest strength and wear resistance. At 350 to 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, coarser ferrite and more austenite give the highest ductility and toughness.
pts: Names the ausferrite matrix: acicular bainitic ferrite with high-carbon (about 2% C) stable retained austenite and no carbides
Si suppresses carbide precipitation, so the rejected carbon stabilises the austenite instead of forming brittle carbide films
Fine ferrite laths raise strength and toughness together (slide 18 lath-width term)
Stable high-carbon austenite: low Ms, strong strain hardening (and transformation under strain), crack blunting
Graphite spheroids act as crack arresters; about twice the strength of ductile iron at the same ductility
Austenitise at 850 to 950^\circ\mathrm{C} in a chloride salt bath; temperature and Si set the matrix carbon
Quench fast into a nitrate salt bath at 250 to 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, missing the pearlite nose
Hold for stage I (about 1 to 2 h) within the processing window, avoiding stage II carbide; air cool, no tempering
Bath temperature: low gives strength and wear resistance, high gives ductility and toughness

8b.watch:
• Do not describe ADI as bainite with carbide. The whole point is the carbide-free ausferrite. Carbide appears only if the hold runs into stage II.
  • Do not temper ADI: tempering decomposes the retained austenite into ferrite and carbide and destroys the toughness.
  • Slide 18 quantifies the strength: YS = \sigma_0 + 1722(\%\mathrm{C})^{1/2} + 115\,d^{-1} + 7.34\times10^{-6}\rho^{1/2} (MPa, d in \mu\mathrm{m}, \rho in \mathrm{m^{-2}}), with UTS about 1.45 times YS. A lower bath temperature gives a smaller lath width d and a higher dislocation density \rho, hence the higher strength.
  • The 900 MPa at 9% elongation figure is ASTM A897 grade 900-650-09, one of several ADI grades.
